title: Sell Mineral Rights in North Dakota
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in North Dakota | Bakken Closings
metaDescription: Most Bakken mineral owners live nowhere near North Dakota. Here's exactly how a remote, out-of-state closing on your Williston Basin interest works.
heroLead: Ask ten North Dakota mineral owners where they live and most of them will name a different state, which is exactly why nonresident closings are the norm here, not the exception.
intro: The Bakken and Three Forks formations under McKenzie, Mountrail, Williams, and Dunn counties turned the Williston Basin into one of the most active oil plays in the country, and the ownership base spread out with it. A lot of Bakken minerals trace back to homesteads and farm estates that split among heirs who scattered across the country over a few generations, so it's routine for a buyer to be closing with a seller who's never set foot in Watford City or Williston and has no plans to.

That reality shapes how these deals actually get done. Nothing about a North Dakota mineral purchase requires you to be in the state, or even to travel anywhere, and understanding how a remote closing is structured will save you from worrying about logistics that simply aren't an issue.

sections.heading: How a nonresident closing actually works
paragraphs: Once you and the buyer agree on a number, the paperwork moves electronically or by mail, whichever you prefer. The mineral deed is drafted to match your recorded interest exactly, sent to you for review, and signed in front of a notary wherever you happen to be, which for most owners means a local bank branch, a UPS Store, or their attorney's office. Some title companies now accept remote online notarization for out-of-state sellers, which lets you complete the notarized signature from home on a video call rather than finding a notary in person, though not every county recorder accepts every form of remote notarization, so your closing agent will confirm what McKenzie or Williams County will record before you go that route.

The signed, notarized deed gets sent back and recorded at the county courthouse in the county where the minerals sit. Funds are held in escrow by a title company or closing attorney until that recording is confirmed clean, then wired or mailed to you. None of this requires you to be physically present in North Dakota at any point.

sections.heading: Why North Dakota title work takes the time it takes
paragraphs: Bakken counties have been busy for over a decade, which is good for confirming recent activity but means the recorder's office is processing a high volume of assignments, leases, and deeds. McKenzie County in particular, centered on Watford City, has seen some of the heaviest drilling activity in the state, and its courthouse workload reflects that. A title search covering your specific tract typically runs back to a clean root of title, often the original homestead patent or a mid-century base lease, and confirms every subsequent transfer lines up.

If your interest passed through an estate that was probated out of state, the title examiner will still need to confirm North Dakota recognizes that probate or that ancillary probate was filed here, since mineral interests are governed by the law of the state where the minerals sit, not where the deceased lived.

sections.heading: Understanding your division order before you sell
paragraphs: If you're currently receiving royalty checks, your division order shows the exact decimal interest an operator is paying you against, tied to a specific spacing unit. Bakken wells are drilled in large horizontal units, often a full section or more, so your decimal interest may look like a small number even on a meaningful mineral position. Pull your most recent division order and a few months of check stubs before requesting an offer, since that documentation lets a buyer value your interest based on actual production history rather than guesswork, and it's the same documentation your buyer's title company will cross-reference at closing.

faqs.question: Do I need to travel to North Dakota to sell my minerals?
faqs.answer: No. Nonresident closings are standard for Bakken minerals. You sign the deed in front of a notary wherever you live, sometimes through remote online notarization, and the deed is mailed or delivered to the county for recording.

faqs.question: How long does a North Dakota mineral closing take?
faqs.answer: Typically three to six weeks. Busy counties like McKenzie and Mountrail have high recording volumes, and if your title traces back through an out-of-state probate, confirming ancillary probate was filed correctly can add time.

faqs.question: What if my mineral interest passed through a will probated in another state?
faqs.answer: North Dakota generally requires the probate to be recognized here, sometimes through ancillary probate, before a deed transferring the minerals can be recorded cleanly. Your buyer's title company will identify this early rather than at the closing table.

faqs.question: Will remote online notarization work for my closing?
faqs.answer: It depends on the specific county recorder's current requirements. Some North Dakota counties accept remote online notarization for out-of-state sellers and others still prefer traditional in-person notarization, so confirm with your closing agent before scheduling.

faqs.question: My decimal interest on the division order looks tiny. Is it still worth selling?
faqs.answer: Small decimal interests are the norm in large Bakken spacing units and are routinely purchased. Value depends on the well's production history and remaining decline curve, not on how large the decimal number looks on paper.
